answer: A place I remember as being incredibly noisy was Chawkbazar, a large wholesale market in Old Dhaka. I went there one morning last year, while I was staying with my elder sister, to help my brother-in-law buy things in bulk for a family wedding, and the sheer volume of sound was overwhelming from the moment we stepped out of the rickshaw. The lanes are extremely narrow, and every inch is filled with shops, porters carrying huge loads on their heads and handcarts squeezing past. Traders were shouting out their prices, customers were haggling loudly, and the constant honking of vehicles added to the [[chaos]]. It was genuinely [[deafening]] at times, and I struggled to hear the person next to me. Yet there was an undeniable energy to it all; the noise felt alive rather than unpleasant. I found the whole scene strangely [[exhilarating]], even if I would not want to be there every day. After a couple of hours, though, I was desperate for some quiet, as the constant [[din]] became exhausting, and I had a slight headache by the time we left. Coming from Sirajganj, which is relatively calm, I was amazed that people work in that environment every single day. Honestly, it gave me a real appreciation for peace and quiet, which I usually [[take for granted]]. It was a fascinating, if overwhelming, glimpse of everyday commerce, and I felt I had seen the real heartbeat of the capital.

followUps.q: Do you mind noisy places in general?
followUps.answer: I can tolerate them for a short while, especially if there is a good reason to be there, but I definitely prefer quiet places. After a long day, noise wears me out far more quickly than hard work.
Not really, compared with Dhaka. There is traffic and plenty of rickshaw bells in the town centre, but the residential area where we live is fairly quiet, especially in the evenings.

note: 'Old part of the city' made Old Dhaka (Chawkbazar), visited while staying with his elder sister; the relative is his brother-in-law; added why it was noisy and a Sirajganj contrast; marked existing 'take for granted'.
